title: NASA Locks In Design of SR-1 Freedom, Its Nuclear-Powered Mars Spacecraft

content:
NASA has locked in key parts of the design of SR-1 Freedom, the nuclear-powered spacecraft it plans to launch in late 2028 to carry three helicopters to Mars, the agency announced on Nov. 24.

SR-1 Freedom — short for Space Reactor-1 — would be the first fission-powered spacecraft to travel beyond Earth orbit, according to NASA. It will use both nuclear and solar power, and it is designed to demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion, in which a reactor generates the electricity that drives the spacecraft’s thrusters, working in deep space for the first time.

The decisions came out of a major design review in October at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland. The boom that keeps the reactor away from the main body of the spacecraft will be shorter than in early drawings, to save weight and make assembly simpler. The design also includes better shielding and bigger antennas.

NASA also gave Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory a $39.3 million contract to design and build the system that sheds the reactor’s waste heat, working with the company Advanced Cooling Technologies.

Once SR-1 Freedom has left Earth orbit, it will switch on its reactor, raise the power gradually and run it for a while, sending performance data home, then shut it down and let the Sun take over. The spacecraft will carry SkyFall, a capsule holding three helicopters that will study Mars’s geology and climate history and look for ice under the surface — following Ingenuity, the first aircraft to fly on another world. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman first presented the idea in March 2026, aiming for a launch in the next Mars window.

If it flies as planned, SR-1 Freedom would prove that a nuclear reactor can power a spacecraft far from the Sun — the kind of technology a future crewed mission to Mars would depend on.

Sources: NASA, Nov. 24, 2026; Mars Progress, Nov. 25, 2026.
